desc:
A tree has n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1. Node i carries the value vals[i], and edges lists its n - 1 two-way connections, so any two nodes are joined by exactly one simple path.

A path is good if its two end nodes have the same value and every node on the path (ends included) has a value that is at most that value. A path made of a single node is good. The paths u → v and v → u count as one path. Return the number of good paths.
constraints: edges.length = n - 1 and the edges form a tree
0 ≤ a, b < n for every edge [a, b]
hints: Checking every pair of equal-valued nodes by walking the path is too slow for a star with thousands of equal nodes. Think about how a path becomes allowed as you raise a threshold.
Process the edges in increasing order of the larger value of their two ends. After processing all edges up to threshold v, each component contains only nodes of value at most v.

Use union-find where every root also remembers the largest value in its component and how many nodes carry it. When two components with the same largest value are merged, add countA * countB new good paths. Start the answer at n for the single-node paths.
editorial: A path is good exactly when its maximum value is attained at both ends. Sort all edges by max(vals[a], vals[b]) and add them one at a time to a union-find structure. When an edge of weight w is added, both of its end components consist only of nodes with value at most w, so any path through the new edge between two nodes of value w has maximum w and is good.

For every component keep the maximum value and the number of nodes holding it. Merging components whose maximums differ simply keeps the larger maximum and its count, since the smaller-valued maxima can no longer be the end of a good path through the merged component. If the maximums are equal, every node with that value in one component pairs with every such node in the other, giving cnta · cntb new good paths, and the counts add. Starting from n single-node paths, the total is the answer. The cost is O(n log n) for the sort plus nearly linear union-find work, and the answer is at most n(n + 1)/2, which fits in 32 bits for n at most 5,000.
